MATERNAL MURDERS

By: Latashia Naidoo | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Is it possible to forgive the unforgivable, especially when it’s a mother who’s taken the lives of her own children?

Unique Selling Point:
Maternal murder cases have been on the increase in South Africa in recent years.
Yet far from experiencing notoriety for their crimes, many of the women who’ve been accused of killing their own children have now started to receive support and sympathy from online communities.

Summary:
This is a story about maternal filicide (mothers who kill their children), with a particular focus on the historical leniency of courts when passing down judgment on these murder-accused, as well as the sympathy these women tend to receive from family members and on social media - in spite of their actions.

Further information:
When Zinhle Maditla murdered her four young children on Christmas Day in 2018, it was a deliberate and calculated act.
The courts saw the punishment of four consecutive life terms as fitting for her crimes.
But many on social media - and especially her own family - disagreed.
What followed was a barrage of support from strangers on Facebook and Twitter, calling for a mistrial, a lighter sentence, and with many claiming that they understood what unemployed single mother Zinhle must’ve been going through when she chose to kill her children.
Some even suggested that the children were spared a life of hardship, because of their mother’s deeds.

This points to a similar pattern of sympathy which has emerged in the case of Dr Lauren Dickason, the South African woman who murdered her three young daughters in New Zealand in 2021.
Following her arrest, numerous Facebook groups have been created in support of Lauren, with people writing to her every week to offer support to the “grieving mother”.
Many have expressed relief that she will receive the best psychiatric help in New Zealand - as opposed to South Africa, and some have even called for her to be exonerated of her crimes.
The online communities that have banded around her have also been quick to chastise any criticism of the murder accused.

We speak to Zinhle’s family and learn about the lives of the Maditla children as they grew up in rural Witbank, and explore the circumstances which led to her taking the lives of the very children she birthed and raised almost single-handedly.
We speak to a psychologist about the nature vs nurture aspect of maternal filicide, and why some women are regarded as victims in these crimes.
And we get a first-hand account of Maditla’s year-long court case - including discussions on her family’s unwavering support for her - from the journalist who’s now writing a book on the murders.
We also speak to a legal expert about why some criminal actions that are beyond the pale of civilised behavior and which one would think unworthy of forgiveness, receive leniency from the courts.

Script:


MATERNAL MURDERS: REVISED

VIZ: Funeral footage - mourners/digging of the graves (leave to play for a few seconds before going into VO) https://twitter.com/my013news/status/1082547439222091776?s=21

VO: It was going to be a blazing hot day in early-January 2019, when Kevin Balance attended the joint funeral of his grandnieces and nephews - children he’d helped raise alongside his own.

UPS KEVIN: 31:48
“I don’t think soon I’ll forget what I saw there. The day of the funeral, it was horrific. That’s why the funeral was so early in the morning - because of the condition of the bodies. You couldn’t have the funeral late, because yoh, they were too much decomposed.”

VIZ: CRIME SCENE FOOTAGE - eNCA police vans, police tape, people crying

VO: Days before, the eMalahleni police had discovered the bodies of the Maditla siblings in a rented one-room home. Minenhle was 8, Blessing, 7, Shaniqua, 3, and Ethen - only 11 months old.

VIZ: ZINHLE IN COURT - walking up from the docks

VO: Their mother, Zinhle, handed herself to police within hours of the discovery.

PAUSE

VIZ: CLAIRE AND KEVIN OUTSIDE THE HOME

VO: It’s been three years since Kevin revisited the tiny room where everything went so very wrong for his family. But he wanted us to see - to remind us of what they endured.

VO: Being back here has magnified his feelings of loss.


VIZ: DAY 1 CAM 1 MVI_0174
KEVIN: 01:56 – 02:10
“I can just see them lying there, begging for their lives, and nobody coming to their rescue. This is becoming very hard.”
CLAIRE LINK –DAY 1 CAM 1 - MV1_0184
“This is the room where Zinhle Maditla lived with her four children. And it’s in this room where they met their tragic fate, after their mother fed them atchar laced with rat poison. It’s also here where relatives found their lifeless bodies wrapped in blankets – four days after they were killed.”
VIZ: COURT FOOTAGE OF ZINHLE SITTING IN COURT CRYING; PEOPLE WAILING AT THE FUNERAL

VO: Zinhle’s actions caused an uproar in her hometown.

VO: Her crime: filicide - the act of a parent deliberately killing their own child.

CLAIRE LINK: MVI_0218
“The tragedy of a child’s death is one that affects the entire community. That tragedy is magnified when the death is at the hands of a family member – in this case, their own mother.

VIZ: CRIME SCENE FOOTAGE OUTSIDE DICKASON HOME - THERE’S SOME GREAT VIZ OF THE CORONER'S VAN, POLICE, COMMUNITY https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vhA6sy7K0wc (USE POLICE STATEMENT TO PLAY BEFORE THE VO - 0”32 “The deceased were children and siblings, two aged 3, and one aged 7..”)

VO: Three years later - in September 2021 - and on the other side of the world, in New Zealand, the same tragedy played itself out in the lives of a family who had just immigrated there from South Africa.

VIZ: USE UPS OF NEIGHBOURS.
DESCRIBING SCENE

VO: Two weeks after Graham Dickason and his family arrived in Timaru, police were called to their new home. Twins Karla and Maya and their older sister Liane - were dead. Strangled with cable ties. Allegedly by their mother.

No-one in the family has recovered enough to even speak to us.

VIZ: UPS OF THOMAS REPORTING FROM THE SCENE - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vhA6sy7K0wc

VO: Thomas Mead covered the scene for 1News New Zealand.

THOMAS MEAD ZOOM 16:48 - 17:10
“One moment that really stuck with me was seeing the hearse leave, and just thinking about how that was the end of their journey; how these three children had come on this huge adventure from the other side of the world, and then left in that hearse. And just watching it drive out - it was a horrible thing.”

VIZ: HAPPY PICS OF THE FAMILY
TOGETHER

VO: With three beautiful children, a house in the suburbs, and successful careers as orthopaedic surgeons, Drs Lauren and Graham Dickason seemed to have it all. But Lauren had stopped taking medication for an undisclosed chronic condition.

UPS THOMAS ZOOM 06:50
“That was the thing that really stuck with New Zealanders, was how could this happen, in such a tragic way, right at the start of a big new adventure.”

VO: Thomas could sense an air of loneliness surrounding the Dickasons following the tragedy.

02:10
“One thing that struck me was how they had no one there - because they had just arrived from South Africa. Normally when you get to a murder scene, there might be friends or family, you might see some hugging or crying outside, that kind of thing as people arrive and find out about the tragedy. But they just had no one.”

VO:
…

CLAIRE LINK: MVI_0233
“Filicide happens with depressing regularity in South Africa – with biological mothers being the primary perpetrators of this crime.”

VO: Filicide studies are ongoing. Statistics show that in 2009, 454 children were killed by their mothers - resulting from abuse, violence, and neglect.

VO: Zinhle Maditla was just 24 years old when she killed her children.

UPS: NEWS FOOTAGE FROM ENCA - https://www.enca.com/news/psyche-killer-moms (00’40 - 00’50 montage of kids pics)


VO: eNCA journalist Slindelo Masikane
feels haunted by what she saw at the
murder scene.

SLI: DAY 2, CAM 1 CLIP MVI_0236 (OVERLAY WITH CRIME SCENE FOOTAGE)
SLI: 09:10
“When we arrived there, the picture that stays in my mind is of the window of the bedroom that was taped with police tape. And you could see the flies in the room, because the kids had - they were rotting; that’s how hot it was.”

VO: After two years of covering the case, Slindelo can’t help but look for parallels between Zinhle and Lauren.

SLI: MV1_0237 14:32 - 14:56
“Here’s another woman - completely different to Zinhle Maditla - whose socio-economic conditions are also completely different. What could’ve pushed her to do that? Is she suffering from a mental illness? It brought up all those questions for me again. I looked beyond the headlines - for me, it’s always “but why?”

VIZ: LOVER FOOTAGE https://www.enca.com/news/psyche-killer-moms (01:40)

VO: In court Zinhle said she’d been triggered by seeing her former lover and the father of two of her babies… with another woman.

COL SEDUMEDI: ZOOM – 11:58 – 12:30
“Spousal revenge filicide, where this type of filicide is used to hurt, punish or retaliate against one’s partner… So in other words, it’s intended to inflict irreversible and permanent pain on the other who I see has wronged me.”

VO: Colonel Doctor Precious Sedumedi researches filicide for the police.

Dr Sedumedi:
“With filicide it is an extreme act of violence that culminates from acts of abuse. So you’ll find there has been a history of abuse within the family, that then led to this eruption or explosion of violence.”

VO: Lauren Dickason’s medical history may only be disclosed in her trial - slated to begin in March next year.

UPS: SEDUMEDI ZOOM - 34:57 - 35:16
“We don’t know if they had marital problems, we don’t know the support she got in New Zealand after they relocated. Was she going to work, or was the husband just working? Is there a history of mental illness from her side? Did she relapse or anything? So there’s a lot of questions for me as well.”

CAM 1 DAY 2 CLAIRE LINK: MVI_0216
“By all accounts, Zinhle Maditla and Lauren Dickason were loving mothers. But filicide is not an act of love.”

VO: Filicide is also about far more than just revenge or even post natal depression. The mothers who do hurt or kill their children could be suffering from paranoid thoughts, auditory hallucinations and irrational behaviour.

VIZ: At gravesite, praying

VO: Kevin Balance still struggles with feelings of guilt when he imagines Zinhle’s children crying for help in her absence.

02:18 – 02:57 KEVIN: “If I knew they were crying, if I just came, maybe I could’ve saved them. I’m blaming myself because I couldn’t tell there was something wrong.”03:56 – 04:13

KEVIN: “It’s very, very hard, I won’t lie to you.”

CLAIRE: Is it time to get out, do you want to leave?”

KEVIN: “Ya, I think it’s better, because ya, I think it’s better.”

VO: While many on social media called Zinhle a ‘monster’, Kevin eventually did choose to forgive her, after he saw her remorse in court. (Remove)

UPS: COURT
USE AUDIO From this clip to cover court footage
KEVIN: 12:45 – 13:10 “The moment she took the stand is when we saw she knows she’s done something wrong, and she knows she has to pay for it…”

VO: Graham Dickason has called his wife “a victim”.

VIZ: Facebook Support Page

VO: And in the months since the Timaru tragedy, support for Lauren Dickason has been growing online.

CREATE VISUAL BREAK INTO DEBBIE..

VO: A similar tragedy that struck the Adlington family from Cape Town 20 years ago could explain what the road ahead might be like for those left behind.

VIZ: DEBBIE SHOWING PICS OF HER KIDS AND HUSBAND IN BOOK

UPS DEBBIE:
NINJAV_s001_s001_t887-SD - 19:59:54:21
“I said where are my three children? He said to me that he’s axed your three children - they are dead. And he said your husband then shot himself, he’s dead.”

VIZ: WALKING THROUGH FOREST BEING REFLECTIVE

VO: Debbie can understand why forgiveness is so hard for some.

DEBBIE T90 - 20:11:10:09:
“As the years have gone I have found that it has got a bit easier to handle. You know, I don’t break down as often as what I used to.
UPS DEBBIE: NINJAV_S001_S001_T888-SD - 20:02:37:17 - 20:03:49:14
“It’s been very difficult, but I’ve had to learn to forgive him. And I mean there are days when I cannot believe that he had the guts and the courage to do what he did…I did it purely because I knew if I didn’t, it would make it harder for me to move on.”

VO: She’s watched the unfolding case in New Zealand and has wanted to reach out to Graham Dickason, if only to encourage him that hope does get restored.

UPS DEBBIE: NINJAV_S001_S001_T890 - 20:10:28:09
“It depends on the individual. I don’t think you ever really heal from something like this. It gets easier as time goes by. As the years go it does get easier to handle. But it’s something that will always be there. And he’ll find he’ll go through the same thing.”

VO: Graham Dickason has since returned to South Africa, while his wife undergoes an 18-month psychiatrist in Canterbury - before she’s expected to be cleared to stand trial.

VIZ: PLAY FOOTAGE OF SENTENCING

KEVIN: MVI_0187 0’11 - 0’31
“As you can see, here our little ones are sleeping. Minenhle, Blessing, Shaniqua and Ethan - they’re in there. This is where we say our final goodbyes to them.”

END HERE
Use Zoom out of graveyard



HAVE TO REPLACE UPS IN SECOND PROMO:
PROMO 2: DAY 2 CAM 1: MVI_0226
They say to err is human, to forgive divine. But is it possible to forgive a crime as inconceivable as murdering your own children?
KEVIN: 12:45 – 13:10 “The moment she took the stand is when we saw she knows she’s done something wrong, and she knows she has to pay for it…”

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Is it possible to forgive the unforgivable, especially when it’s a mother who’s taken the lives of her own children?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Maternal murder cases have been on the increase in South Africa in recent years. Yet far from experiencing notoriety for their crimes, many of the women who’ve been accused of killing their own children have now started to receive support and sympathy from online communities.
metadata.Summary: This is a story about maternal filicide (mothers who kill their children), with a particular focus on the historical leniency of courts when passing down judgment on these murder-accused, as well as the sympathy these women tend to receive from family members and on social media - in spite of their actions.
metadata.Further information: When Zinhle Maditla murdered her four young children on Christmas Day in 2018, it was a deliberate and calculated act. The courts saw the punishment of four consecutive life terms as fitting for her crimes. But many on social media - and especially her own family - disagreed. What followed was a barrage of support from strangers on Facebook and Twitter, calling for a mistrial, a lighter sentence, and with many claiming that they understood what unemployed single mother Zinhle must’ve been going through when she chose to kill her children. Some even suggested that the children were spared a life of hardship, because of their mother’s deeds. This points to a similar pattern of sympathy which has emerged in the case of Dr Lauren Dickason, the South African woman who murdered her three young daughters in New Zealand in 2021. Following her arrest, numerous Facebook groups have been created in support of Lauren, with people writing to her every week to offer support to the “grieving mother”. Many have expressed relief that she will receive the best psychiatric help in New Zealand - as opposed to South Africa, and some have even called for her to be exonerated of her crimes. The online communities that have banded around her have also been quick to chastise any criticism of the murder accused. We speak to Zinhle’s family and learn about the lives of the Maditla children as they grew up in rural Witbank, and explore the circumstances which led to her taking the lives of the very children she birthed and raised almost single-handedly. We speak to a psychologist about the nature vs nurture aspect of maternal filicide, and why some women are regarded as victims in these crimes. And we get a first-hand account of Maditla’s year-long court case - including discussions on her family’s unwavering support for her - from the journalist who’s now writing a book on the murders. We also speak to a legal expert about why some criminal actions that are beyond the pale of civilised behavior and which one would think unworthy of forgiveness, receive leniency from the courts.
